readerTitle: The rule that fixed one mistake and slowed everything else
caseNote: 가상 사례 (B2B 마케팅 에이전시, 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 연구 (WHO 수술 안전 체크리스트, Haynes et al. 2009)
insight: 프로세스는 많고 적음이 아니라 위치의 문제다. 자주 반복되고 실수 비용이 큰 지점에만 짧게 넣는다.
misconception: 회사가 커지면 실수가 날 때마다 규칙을 더해야 한다. 반대로, 프로세스는 스타트업의 속도를 죽이니 최대한 피해야 한다.

sources.text: Haynes, A. B., et al. (2009). A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population. New England Journal of Medicine, 360(5), 491–499.
Gawande, A. (2009). The Checklist Manifesto. Metropolitan Books.
에이전시와 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: WHO 체크리스트 연구 수치 확인 필요: 8개 도시 8개 병원, 사망률 1.5% → 0.8%, 주요 합병증 11.0% → 7.0%, 체크리스트 19개 항목. 원문(NEJM 2009) 표와 대조하세요.
에이전시 사례 수치(제안서 2일 → 6일)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
이후 다른 국가·병원에서 체크리스트 효과가 작거나 없었다는 연구도 있습니다(예: 캐나다 온타리오 연구, Urbach et al. 2014, NEJM). 7번 카드의 '실제로 쓰일 때만 효과' 문장의 근거로 출처 추가 여부를 검토하세요.

cards.title: The rule that fixed one mistake and slowed everything else
body: A 25-person marketing agency sent a client an invoice for the wrong amount. The client was annoyed. The founder was embarrassed.
Her fix: every invoice now needs three sign-offs. The wrong invoices stopped. So did on-time invoices. Cash started arriving weeks later.

image.label: An invoice waiting in a queue of three signature boxes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 송장 한 장이 책상 세 개를 차례로 거쳐 가며, 각 책상마다 서명 칸과 쌓인 서류 더미. 마지막 책상 옆 달력이 몇 주 넘어가 있음. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A client report went out with a wrong number.
body: You run a growing B2B consulting firm. Last week, a monthly client report included last quarter's sales figure by mistake. The client caught it.
It's the first time this has happened. What do you do?

options.text: Require a manager to review every report before it goes out
options.feedback: It would catch this error, but it puts every report, risky or not, behind one busy person. You trade one rare mistake for a permanent slowdown.

options.text: Find out why it happened, and add a short check only at the step where numbers get copied in
options.feedback: You fix the actual weak point at low cost. Everyone else keeps moving at the same speed.

options.text: Apologize, fix it, and add nothing. People make mistakes
options.feedback: This protects speed, and for a true one-off it may be fine. But if the copy step is fragile, the error will come back.

cards.title: Rules pile up after every scare.
body: Back at the agency, the invoice rule was only the start. After a typo in a pitch, every proposal needed the founder's review. After a missed deadline, every project needed a weekly status form.
Each rule made sense alone. Together, proposals that used to leave in 2 days now took 6. The agency lost a pitch to a smaller rival who replied first.
Nobody decided to become slow. It happened **one reasonable rule at a time**.

cards.title: Adding process
body: **Process** is a set way of doing repeated work, so the result doesn't depend on someone remembering.
Good process is cheap insurance. It sits exactly where mistakes are likely and costly, and costs a few seconds. Bad process is a reaction to one bad day, applied to everyone, forever.
The question isn't *more or less process*. It's *where*.

image.label: A narrow gate placed only at the risky step of a workflow
image.brief: 업무 흐름을 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 흐르는 길로 표현. 대부분 구간은 넓고 빠르게 열려 있고, 단 한 곳 '위험 구간'에만 작은 체크 게이트. 대비용으로 아래에 모든 구간마다 게이트가 있는 막힌 길.

cards.title: Nineteen checkboxes that saved lives.
body: If process only slows things down, surgery should prove it. Surgeons are skilled, busy and proud.

Yet in a 2008 study across eight hospitals in eight cities, teams used a short WHO checklist of 19 items: confirm the patient, the site, allergies, expected blood loss. Deaths after surgery fell from 1.5% to 0.8%. Major complications fell from 11% to 7%.
The checklist worked because it was short and placed at moments where a skipped step is catastrophic.

cards.title: Ask two questions: how often, and how costly?
body: Process pays when a mistake is both repeated and expensive. Elsewhere, judgment is usually cheaper.
cards.softwareNote: In software, this is why teams automate tests for login and payments but let people ship copy changes freely. The check goes where a mistake hurts customers most.

cards.title: Rules are easy to add and hard to remove.
body: Every rule outlives the problem that created it. Give each one an owner and a date to review it. If nobody can say what it prevents, drop it.

Process also works only when people actually use it. Later studies found smaller or no effects from the same surgical checklist where teams just ticked boxes. A form filled in on autopilot is cost without protection.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your 40-person company sells scheduling software. Twice this quarter, a release broke the payment page for about an hour. Most releases are small text and layout changes.
What process do you add?

options.text: Every release needs sign-off from the head of engineering
options.feedback: Payment outages would likely drop, but so would your release speed. Small, safe changes now wait in line with risky ones.

options.text: Automated tests on payments, plus a short checklist only for changes that touch payments
options.feedback: The check lands exactly where a repeated, costly failure happens. Everything else ships as fast as before.

options.text: Hold a meeting after each outage to discuss what went wrong
options.feedback: You'll learn the cause, which is useful. But two repeats suggest talking alone won't stop the third.

cards.title: Put process where mistakes repeat and hurt.
body: Not after every bad day, and not everywhere. A short check at the right step beats a long one at every step.
**Try it today:** list three rules your team follows. For each, write what mistake it prevents and how often that mistake happened. Cut one that has no answer.
